opus-5.5.text:
I think this is one of the most underrated questions in building a frontier model team, and honestly there isn't a fixed ratio that works everywhere. But I do have a fairly strong view: research compute is not a luxury you allocate after training is taken care of. It's what decides whether your big training run is worth doing at all.

The way I think about it, the final large-scale training run is more like *executing* a decision. By the time you launch it, most of the important choices are already locked in: the architecture, the data mixture, the tokenizer, the learning-rate schedule, how you handle long context, and so on. If those choices are wrong, no amount of GPUs in the final run will save you. You just burn the money faster. So the quality of the big run depends heavily on how much you explored and validated beforehand, at small and medium scale.

That's why I think many teams under-invest in research compute. When resources are tight, the instinct is to put everything into the main run because it's visible and has a deadline. But then researchers are stuck. They can't run enough ablations, they can't test ideas at a scale where the results actually transfer, and in the end they rely on intuition or copy what others have published. Then you lose the chance to find something genuinely better.

In practice, I'd like a meaningful share of compute protected for research, not just the leftovers. And it shouldn't all be tiny experiments. You need a ladder: lots of cheap small-scale runs to filter ideas quickly, then fewer medium-scale runs to check whether a result holds as you scale up. A lot of ideas look great at small scale and disappear at larger scale, and the reverse happens too. If you skip that middle rung, you get fooled.

Another point is that the boundary isn't completely clean. A well-designed main run can also produce research value: checkpoints you can analyze, scaling behavior you can learn from, data-quality signals. And good research infrastructure makes every GPU-hour more efficient. If your experiments are reproducible and your evaluation is reliable, you need far fewer runs to reach a conclusion. So part of the "allocation" problem is really an efficiency problem.

Finally, it's about culture as much as numbers. If researchers feel compute is something they have to beg for, they become conservative and only try safe ideas. If they have a reasonable, predictable budget, they're willing to take risks, and real breakthroughs usually come from those risky bets. So my answer is: protect research compute deliberately, structure it so results transfer to scale, and treat the main training run as the payoff of good research, not as a replacement for it.

r001.rationale: The response recommends protecting a meaningful share of compute for research, but it gives no three-to-five-times ratio or equivalent comparison with actual training.

fable-5.1.text:
This is actually a question I think about a lot, because it's one of the places where the real strategy of a lab shows up. Everyone says they value research, but you can tell what a team actually values by looking at where the compute goes.

My view is that you can't treat it as a fixed percentage. It depends on where you are. If you're in a phase where you already know the recipe and you're mostly scaling, then of course the bulk of compute goes to the big training run, because that's where the model gets made. But if you're in a phase where you don't yet know what works, and honestly most of the time you don't, then starving research of GPUs is the most expensive mistake you can make. You'll end up spending a huge amount of compute on a large run that bakes in a bad decision you could have caught with a small experiment.

So I like to think of it as a pipeline rather than a split. Small-scale experiments should be cheap and fast, and there should be a lot of them, with a clear path for a result to graduate to mid-scale validation and then into the main run. The job of the research compute is to de-risk the training compute. If an idea can't show something at a small scale with proper scaling laws behind it, it generally shouldn't be consuming the big cluster.

The thing I'd really push back on is the mindset that research compute is a cost and training compute is the investment. In practice, it's the opposite. The large run is just executing whatever your research told you to do. If the research is thin, the large run is just a very expensive way to confirm you don't know enough yet.

And there's a cultural piece too. If researchers have to fight for every GPU, they stop taking risks and only propose things they're sure will work, which is exactly what you don't want. Give people enough room to be wrong a few times. That's how you find the thing that's actually worth scaling.

r001.rationale: The response favors substantial research compute and says allocation depends on the phase, but it does not recommend allocating roughly three to five times as many GPUs to research as to training.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate exploratory research from large-scale training, while making sure the two stay closely connected. Research needs a stable allocation of GPUs so people can test ideas quickly. If every experiment has to wait for a major training run to finish, you slow down the work that could make the next run better.

At the same time, large-scale training needs concentrated resources. Spreading GPUs across too many projects can leave everyone moving slowly. So I wouldn’t set a fixed ratio. I’d protect a baseline for research and adjust the rest according to the stage of development.

The key is deciding which experiments deserve to scale up. Start with smaller tests, establish whether an idea works, and then commit more compute. A useful research result can save a lot of training resources, but it also needs to hold up at scale.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly rejects a fixed ratio and recommends a protected research baseline with the remaining GPUs adjusted to development stage; it does not recommend three to five times as many GPUs for research as for training.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d divide resources according to the stage of the work, rather than set a fixed ratio. Early on, researchers need enough GPUs to test ideas quickly and establish which improvements are reliable. Once a direction is validated, we can commit more resources to a large training run.

I’d also protect some capacity for research during training. Otherwise, one big run can occupy the entire cluster and leave everyone waiting. The goal is to keep experiments moving while giving major training runs the stable resources they need.

r001.rationale: The response recommends stage-based allocation and reserving some capacity for research, but it does not state or imply a research-to-training ratio of roughly 3–5 to 1.
